lessons.title: 1 · Count objects, keep the amount
lessons.goal: Count each object once, recognize zero, and compare quantities without relying on their spacing.
lessons.materials: Paper and pencil. Draw marks for objects, or use large paper cards. A helper can read the text aloud. These are supported introductions, not an audio course or a complete early-mathematics curriculum.
paragraphs:
START WITH SOMETHING YOU CAN COUNT
Draw four separate marks. Point to one mark as you say each number: one, two, three, four. Move a finger or pencil tip to the next uncounted mark each time. The last number you say tells how many marks there are. Writing the digit 4 records that amount.

MAKE THE COUNT CHECKABLE
Keep counted and uncounted objects separate: move a card to a counted pile, or make a light tick beside each mark. Do not count an object twice and do not skip one. Count again in a different order to check. You should get the same total if no objects were added or removed.

WORKED EXAMPLE · TWO ROWS, ONE COLLECTION
There are four marks in one row and three in another. Touch all four in the first row, saying 1, 2, 3, 4. Continue through the second row: 5, 6, 7. There are seven marks altogether. If you move them into one row, there are still seven; the arrangement changes, not the amount.

ZERO AND COMPARISON
Zero means there are none of the objects being counted. An empty box holds zero cards, not one card because there is one box. To compare two collections, match one object from the first with one from the second. If one collection has objects left over, it has more. A longer-looking row can have fewer objects if they are spread farther apart.

A MISTAKE TO EXPLAIN
Someone counts five cards but says six because one card was touched twice. The problem is the matching of number words to objects. Recount while moving each card once; do not merely choose a different last number. A counting method should let another person see why every card was counted exactly once.

TRY, EXPLAIN, REVISIT
Use the practice card below. Enter just the number for numeric questions. For writing tasks, explain or describe a drawing; a helper can type your spoken explanation. Later, draw a new collection of up to ten marks and check it in a different order.

PRACTICE CARD
COUNTING CARD — ORIGINAL PAPER PRACTICE
[N1] Row A: five marks, written as | | | | |. Row B: three marks, written as | | |. Count marks, not the spaces between them.
[N2] A third box is empty: it contains no marks.
[N3] Eight cards are moved from a short row into a long row. No cards are added or removed.
[N4] Collection P has six cards; collection Q has four cards. Match one P card to one Q card until one collection is used up.

hints: Start with A's five marks.
Continue the count for B's three marks instead of restarting your total.
mistakes: Five counts only row A. Include the marks in B too.
Check that each of the eight marks is counted once; count marks rather than gaps.

lessons.title: 2 · Tens and ones: the value of a digit
lessons.goal: Represent a two-digit number with tens and ones, trade one ten for ten ones, and explain a zero in the ones place.
lessons.materials: Paper and pencil. Draw marks for objects, or use large paper cards. A helper can read the text aloud. These are supported introductions, not an audio course or a complete early-mathematics curriculum.
paragraphs:
BUILD A TEN
Draw ten small marks and circle the group. Call that group one ten. It still contains ten ones. A ten-rod in the diagram is divided into ten cells to show this relationship. One rod and one loose circle do not have the same value: the rod represents ten ones, the circle one.

CONNECT GROUPS TO WRITTEN NUMBERS
In a two-digit whole number, the left digit tells the number of tens and the right digit tells the number of ones. In 24, the 2 means two tens, or twenty. The 4 means four ones. Together they make twenty-four. The digit's position is part of its meaning; 24 and 42 are different amounts.

WORKED EXAMPLE · TRADE WITHOUT CHANGING THE AMOUNT
Start with two tens and four ones: 24. Open one of the tens into ten loose ones. Now there is one ten and fourteen ones. The amount is still 24 because nothing was added or removed. Regroup ten of those loose ones into a rod to return to two tens and four ones.

WHY ZERO HAS A JOB
Thirty is three tens and no loose ones. Write 30 so the 3 stays in the tens place and the 0 records no ones. Writing 3 instead would mean three ones. Zero can record an empty place; it is not an instruction to erase that place.

WORKED COMPARISON
Compare 24 with 42. Two tens are fewer than four tens, so 24 is smaller. Compare tens before ones for these two-digit numbers. If the tens are equal, compare the ones: 24 is smaller than 27 because they both have two tens and four ones are fewer than seven.

TRY AND CHECK
Build the practice amounts with drawn ten-rods and single marks. Count the value of the rods, not only how many shapes you drew. Explain a trade in your own words, then check by counting every represented one.

PRACTICE CARD
PLACE-VALUE CARD — ORIGINAL PAPER PRACTICE
[P1] A collection has three tens and six ones. Each ten contains ten ones.
[P2] Another collection has four tens and zero loose ones.
[P3] A drawing has two tens and thirteen loose ones.
[P4] In the written number 52, the 5 is in the tens place and the 2 is in the ones place.

questions.prompt: What number is represented by P1?
questions.explanation: Three tens represent 30 ones. Add the six loose ones to get 36. The 3 belongs in the tens place and the 6 in the ones place.
hints: Count 10, 20, 30 for the rods.
After thirty, count the six loose ones.
mistakes: Three rods plus six circles are nine shapes, but each rod represents ten ones.
You reversed tens and ones: P1 has three tens, not six.

lessons.title: 3 · Addition: combine and regroup
lessons.goal: Add by counting on or making a ten, and explain why regrouping preserves the sum.
lessons.materials: Paper and pencil. Draw marks for objects, or use large paper cards. A helper can read the text aloud. These are supported introductions, not an audio course or a complete early-mathematics curriculum.
paragraphs:
WHAT ADDITION ASKS
Addition can combine two collections. If there are six cards and three more arrive, count all the cards or start at six and count on three steps: seven, eight, nine. The starting six is not the first new card. Write 6 + 3 = 9; the equals sign means the amounts on its two sides are the same.

WORKED EXAMPLE · MAKE A TEN
For 8 + 5, split the five into two and three. Eight plus two makes ten; three remain to add. Ten plus three is thirteen. You moved part of the five into a convenient group; you did not add an extra two. A sketch can show eight marks joined by two of the five, with three left outside the ten.

WORKED EXAMPLE · TWO-DIGIT SUM
Add 27 and 15. Two tens plus one ten make three tens. Seven ones plus five ones make twelve ones. Three tens and twelve ones represent 42, because ten of those ones can be regrouped into a fourth ten with two ones left. The diagram steps show the two starting amounts, the combined groups, and the regrouped sum.

CONNECT TO THE WRITTEN METHOD
When writing 27 + 15 in columns, line up ones under ones and tens under tens. The ones sum is twelve: record two ones and carry one ten into the tens column. That carried 1 represents ten ones, not one extra loose one. The tens column now has 2 + 1 + 1 = 4 tens.

CHECK THE SIZE AND THE STORY
Adding a positive number makes a whole-number amount larger. A sum smaller than either positive starting amount needs checking. Estimate 27 + 15 as about 30 + 10, or 40, then check the exact 42 with the diagram. An estimate is a rough check, not a replacement for the exact answer requested.

YOUR TURN
Use new numbers in Practice. Draw the tens and ones before using a written shortcut. Name the value of every carried digit. Later, invent an addition with more than nine ones in its combined ones column and explain the regrouping to someone else.

PRACTICE CARD
ADDITION CARD — ORIGINAL PAPER PRACTICE
[A1] There are eight cards. Five more cards arrive.
[A2] One pile has 26 cards and another has 17. Both piles are combined.
[A3] A starting pile of nine cards must become a pile of fourteen cards.
[A4] In 26 + 17, the ones add to thirteen: one ten and three ones.

lessons.title: 4 · Subtraction: remove or find the gap
lessons.goal: Subtract whole numbers with a clear model, regroup a ten when needed, and check by addition.
lessons.materials: Paper and pencil. Draw marks for objects, or use large paper cards. A helper can read the text aloud. These are supported introductions, not an audio course or a complete early-mathematics curriculum.
paragraphs:
TWO USEFUL MEANINGS
Subtraction can ask what remains after removal: 11 cards with 4 removed leaves 7. It can also ask for a gap: how many more are needed to go from 4 to 11? That gap is 7. In both cases 11 − 4 = 7, and 4 + 7 = 11 checks the relationship.

WORKED EXAMPLE · CROSS A TEN
For 13 − 5, remove three to reach ten, then remove two more because 3 + 2 = 5. Eight remain. You must remove five altogether, not three and then another five. Drawing thirteen marks and crossing out exactly five checks the result.

WORKED EXAMPLE · REGROUP BEFORE REMOVING
For 42 − 17, start with four tens and two ones. You need to remove seven ones, but only two are loose. Exchange one ten for ten ones. Now you have three tens and twelve ones, still 42. Remove one ten and seven ones. Two tens and five ones remain: 25.

WHY THE TENS CHANGE
Opening a ten does not create ten new ones for free. The tens count decreases by one when the ones count increases by ten. In 42, four tens and two ones become three tens and twelve ones. Keeping four tens as well would incorrectly model 52.

CHECK WITH ADDITION
A subtraction answer should make the related addition true. For 42 − 17 = 25, check 17 + 25 = 42. This catches the common error of subtracting the smaller digit from the larger separately in each column. The original amount and the amount removed determine the order.

TRY A MODEL FIRST
In Practice, name what you start with, what you remove, and what remains. Some tasks ask for a gap rather than removal. Use the same addition check for both. Draw a new regrouping example later and explain why opening one ten preserves the starting amount.

PRACTICE CARD
SUBTRACTION CARD — ORIGINAL PAPER PRACTICE
[S1] Start with thirteen cards and remove five.
[S2] Start with 43 cards and remove 18. A ten can be opened into ten ones.
[S3] One person has nine cards and needs sixteen altogether.
[S4] A proposed solution to 43 − 18 is 35: its writer took 8 − 3 in the ones column and 4 − 1 in the tens column.

questions.prompt: How many cards remain in S1?
questions.explanation: Remove three from thirteen to reach ten, then remove the remaining two to reach eight. Check 8 + 5 = 13.
hints: Split the removal of five into three and two.
After reaching ten, remove only the two still needed.
mistakes: Adding five increases the collection. S1 removes five.
If counting backward, count five moves after thirteen; the starting thirteen is not a move.

lessons.title: 5 · Multiplication: equal groups
lessons.goal: Represent equal groups with repeated addition and multiplication, and distinguish the number of groups from the size of each group.
lessons.materials: Paper and pencil. Draw marks for objects, or use large paper cards. A helper can read the text aloud. These are supported introductions, not an audio course or a complete early-mathematics curriculum.
paragraphs:
START WITH THE GROUPS
Draw three boxes and put four marks in each. You have three equal groups of four. Count by groups: 4, 8, 12. The repeated addition is 4 + 4 + 4 = 12. In this course, 3 × 4 describes three groups with four in each. State your group convention when explaining a model.

WHAT THE TWO NUMBERS DO
One number tells how many groups; the other tells how many objects are in each group. Do not add those two counts to find the total objects. Three boxes of four cards do not contain 3 + 4 cards; the four-card group occurs three times.

WORKED EXAMPLE · AN ARRAY
Arrange twelve marks in three rows of four. Each row is a group. Turn the paper and you can see four rows of three, still twelve marks. This helps explain why 3 × 4 and 4 × 3 have the same total, even though a story about three boxes with four each names the groups differently.

WORKED EXAMPLE · BREAK A GROUP COUNT APART
For 5 groups of 6, first count 4 groups: 6 + 6 + 6 + 6 = 24. One more group adds 6, giving 30. Splitting a harder count into known groups is useful if you keep all groups and do not count any twice.

ZERO, ONE AND UNEQUAL GROUPS
Zero groups of five cards have no cards: 0 × 5 = 0. One group of five has five: 1 × 5 = 5. If groups have different sizes, a statement such as 'four in every group' is false. You can still add their actual sizes; do not assume equality merely because their total happens to match an equal-group model.

TRY AND EXPLAIN
Draw each group before calculating the total. Label both the group count and objects per group. After the questions, invent a different group story with the same total and explain what changed and what stayed the same.

lessons.title: 6 · Division: sharing, groups and leftovers
lessons.goal: Distinguish sharing among groups from making groups of a given size, interpret whole-object remainders, and check with multiplication.
lessons.materials: Paper and pencil. Draw marks for objects, or use large paper cards. A helper can read the text aloud. These are supported introductions, not an audio course or a complete early-mathematics curriculum.
paragraphs:
SHARE EQUALLY
Sharing 12 cards among 3 people asks how many cards each person receives. Deal one card to each person, then repeat until all cards are used. Each receives four. Write 12 ÷ 3 = 4 and check: 3 people × 4 cards each = 12 cards. Equal sharing means the recipients receive the same number.

MAKE GROUPS OF A GIVEN SIZE
Packing 12 cards with 3 in each envelope asks how many envelopes can be filled. Make one group of three at a time. Four full envelopes result. The arithmetic 12 ÷ 3 = 4 is the same, but the answer now counts envelopes rather than cards per person. Label the answer from the story.

WORKED EXAMPLE · WHOLE-CARD LEFTOVERS
Pack 14 cards in envelopes holding exactly four cards each. Three full envelopes use 3 × 4 = 12 cards; two cards remain. A fourth full envelope would need four cards, so the two are a remainder. Check: 3 × 4 + 2 = 14, and the remainder 2 is smaller than the group size 4.

WHAT TO DO WITH THE REMAINDER
The question determines how to report leftovers. If it asks for full four-card packs, the answer is three packs with two cards left. If it asks for enough envelopes to hold all fourteen with at most four each, you need four envelopes, one partly filled. If objects can be divided into smaller parts, fractions may be appropriate; these questions specify whole cards.

WHY ZERO GROUP SIZE FAILS
Making groups of zero cards never uses any of a positive collection. There is no group count that satisfies 'number of groups × 0 = 12'. So 12 ÷ 0 is not a valid whole-number answer. This differs from sharing zero cards among three people: each receives zero.

CONNECT AND CONTINUE
Use Practice to name the group size, group count and remainder. Check that full groups plus leftovers reproduce the starting amount. After this course, choose Guided: Measure & plan for fractions and measurement. Equal-group language will help you discuss the equal parts of a stated whole.

PRACTICE CARD
DIVISION CARD — ORIGINAL PAPER PRACTICE
[D1] Eighteen whole cards are shared equally among three people; all cards are shared.
[D2] Seventeen whole cards are packed into full groups of five cards. Do not split a card.
[D3] To hold every one of those seventeen cards, each envelope may hold at most five cards and the last may be partly filled.
[D4] Zero cards are shared among three people. A different proposed task tries to make zero-card groups from twelve cards.
